task: Escribe un artículo breve (130–160 palabras) con consejos para usar el celular de forma más consciente. Incluye al menos una oración con the more..., the more... y otra en voz pasiva.
paragraphs: In 1971, the economist Herbert Simon made an observation that sounds remarkably modern: "a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention." Half a century later, his words have become the foundation of one of the most profitable business models in history.

Many of the apps we use every day are free. Social networks, video platforms and news sites do not charge us a penny. Instead, they make money by selling advertising, and advertisers pay for one thing above all: our time and attention. The longer we stay, the more adverts we see, and the more data the company collects about our interests. This is what critics call the "attention economy".

To keep us engaged, designers use techniques borrowed from psychology. Infinite scrolling removes natural stopping points, so there is never a moment when we reach the end. Notifications arrive at unpredictable moments, which, like a slot machine, makes us check our phones again and again. Videos start playing automatically, and recommendation algorithms learn which content keeps each individual hooked, which is often content that makes us angry or anxious.

Some former employees of technology companies have become outspoken critics of these practices. They argue that products designed to capture as much attention as possible may damage our ability to concentrate, our sleep and even public debate, since outrage spreads faster than calm reflection.

The companies reply that they give users tools to control their screen time, and that people are free to choose what they watch. It is also worth remembering that worries about new media are not new: similar fears were expressed about novels, radio and television.

Still, many people are looking for ways to take back control. Some switch off all non-essential notifications or turn their screens grey, which makes them less attractive. Others keep their phones out of the bedroom. None of these strategies is perfect, but they share a simple idea: attention is a limited resource, and it is worth deciding consciously where we spend it.
